Is JD Vance's Iran deal gambit a career-maker — or a career-ender?

JD Vance took the White House podium Thursday to defend the US-Iran deal, a move that has positioned him as the public face of an agreement widely panned by conservatives. Whether this gambit helps or hurts his political future — especially a potential 2028 presidential run — depends entirely on which way the wind blows over the next 60 days.

The vice president is already taking incoming fire from his own party. Commentator Ben Shapiro flatly declared "this is JD's deal" and said Vance "has not well served the president". Senator Bill Cassidy called it the "worst foreign policy blunder in decades", while Senator Ted Cruz blasted the "very, very poor advice" the president is receiving — a clear jab at Vance.

Trump himself has set Vance up as the fall guy. "If it works out, I'm going to take the credit. If it doesn't work out, I'm blaming JD," the president joked — though few are laughing. One Republican strategist called it "classic Trump to throw JD under the bus".

The political risks are compounded by Vance's potential 2028 rival, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who has conspicuously stayed out of the spotlight and positioned himself to avoid blame if the deal collapses.

On the other hand, Vance is betting that voters will reward him for ending an unpopular war. If the countries reach a final agreement that actually curbs Iran's nuclear program, he'll have played a central role in achieving a longtime US goal.

Some allies insist he can emerge stronger. Senator Kevin Cramer noted the deal "adds to the national security and geopolitical chops" of Vance . And a White House source argued that "there's no real downside risk to the president and vice president for giving the peace process a chance". 

Vance is walking a tightrope with no net. He has wagered his career on defending Trump's policies — including this deal. If it works, he's a peacemaker. If it fails, he's a fall guy.

Given the deal is already on life support — with negotiations postponed indefinitely and both Trump and Vance offering contradictory statements on key provisions — the smart money says this gamble will hurt more than help.

💬 Iran slams US proposal to reallocate frozen assets to regional allies

📌 Tehran, IRNA – The High Council of Human Rights (HCHR) has strongly condemned remarks by the US Treasury secretary suggesting that Iranian state assets could be used to compensate some of Washington's regional allies for alleged damage caused in the recent US-Israeli war on Iran, calling the proposal a violation of international law and the principles governing relations between sovereign states.

In a statement released on Saturday, the HCHR said any attempt to seize, transfer, or allocate assets belonging to the Iranian nation would constitute a breach of the internationally recognized principle of sovereign immunity, which protects states and their property from unilateral confiscation by other countries.
​
Iran’s top rights body argued that no state has the legal authority to unilaterally decide how another country's assets should be used, describing such measures as contrary to the rule of law and international legal obligations.
​
The statement also said that the seizure or confiscation of national assets, particularly when combined with unilateral sanctions and other coercive economic measures, has far-reaching humanitarian consequences.
​
The council noted that United Nations special rapporteurs and other UN human rights mechanisms have repeatedly warned about the harmful impact of unilateral coercive measures and extraterritorial economic restrictions on the fundamental rights of nations.
​
Rejecting any potential move to dispose of or reallocate Iranian assets, the statement said the United States would bear full legal and international responsibility for the consequences of any such action. It added that Iran reserves the right to pursue the matter through all available legal and international mechanisms.
